prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated together, bringing atomic clocks to the 1e-18 level

statement.case_for: After reading all eight round-1 statements and the chair's questions, I keep the optical lattice clock (B009) as the whole configuration. It satisfies the test I apply to every candidate: an original invention, experimentally verified, that opens a door. The new element is the magic-wavelength lattice: the light shift cancels for the clock transition, so thousands of atoms are held Doppler- and recoil-free and interrogated at once. That is neither the 2005 frequency comb nor the 2012 control of single ions. It is the step that made both statistical power and the Lamb-Dicke regime available together. Verification is what persuades me most. Sr, Yb and Hg clocks in Tokyo, Boulder, Paris and Braunschweig agree in international comparisons at the 1e-18 level, so the systematics are understood and not just claimed. It has also produced physics: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on constant drift and dark-matter couplings, and many-body spin-exchange effects in the lattice. I would word the citation around the invention and realization of the lattice clock, with the 1e-18 figure as a descriptive consequence. The redefinition of the second should not appear in it, since Pearce is right that it is a consequence and has not happened. On credit, the roles of the two names are separable: Katori proposed and first realized the scheme, and Ye took it to record accuracy and stability and opened the many-body side. Several colleagues have said this independently, and Lindroth reports that within the atomic community Katori's priority for the magic-wavelength concept is not seriously contested. I still note that no file checks this independently.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is real, and all eight of us raised it. I do not think it is disqualifying, but the committee should be able to state in one sentence why this is a distinct invention, and the citation wording above is my attempt at that. My second reservation is that this is an instrument whose consequences are still partly prospective. No departure from known physics has been seen (Johansson), and the redefinition of the second is pending (Kroll, Pearce). A prize that reads as a prize for better numbers would be the lifetime-achievement trap I want to avoid, which is why I want the citation tied to the invention and not to accuracy as such. Third, credit beyond two names is a real cost. Lemonde and SYRTE, Ludlow and Oates, Takamoto, Hinkley, Bloom, Lisdat and PTB, and Derevianko's magic-wavelength theory all contributed, and a two-name citation leaves them out. That is unavoidable under the three-name limit and the verified record, but it is a loss and I do not want to hide it. Finally, I am still relying on the supplied files and general knowledge for who demonstrated what first. I would support asking an outside clock-metrology reviewer to confirm Katori's proposal and first demonstration, and the specific lattice-clock milestones credited to Ye as distinct from the wider JILA programme, before the final vote.

responses.point: Eriksson moved from B018 to B009 but is still less relaxed about the 2012 ion-clock precedent than the 2005 comb prize, and still has the lattice clock as a refinement of an honoured lineage in the back of mind.
responses.response: I think the 2012 overlap is the harder of the two, and I do not want to wave it away. The 2012 prize honoured manipulating and measuring individual quantum systems, and ion clocks followed from that. The lattice clock is a different physical solution to the same problem. Neutral atoms in large numbers, held where the light shift cancels, trade the single ion's isolation for statistics. It was not an obvious extension of ion control, and the ion groups did not make it. That is why I regard it as a new invention and not a refinement. I also thank you for the candid assessment of B018. We agree it is not ready to lead, since the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal sits outside the three names and the 2016 prize leaves overlap to argue. If the committee wants a materials-based reserve, I think B019 and B018 are both still short of a clean credit, and I would rather say so than force one.

responses.point: Pearce asks whether Ye's decisive contribution is the lattice clock itself or the wider JILA programme, and whether Hall's 2005 role bears on allocation. He also says the citation should not depend on the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree on the citation, and I have changed my own wording to drop any dependence on the redefinition. On Ye, my reading is that the claim for the lattice clock itself is concrete: the strontium lattice clock reaching the 1e-18 regime, the stability that allowed millimetre-scale redshift measurements within a sample, and the many-body shifts understood in that platform. Comb-linked spectroscopy and spin-exchange physics are neighbouring parts of the programme and I would keep them out of the citation. Hall's 2005 prize honoured the comb and precision spectroscopy and is a separate prize, so it limits what we can say about the comb but does not take the lattice clock's invention away from the two named people. I still want the lattice-clock record checked by an outside reviewer on this point. I also appreciate your frankness that atomic physics is outside your expertise, and I would ask that the verification be put to a specialist.

responses.point: Danielsson worries that a prize about better numbers risks looking incremental, and sees the pending redefinition of the second as making the timing right.
responses.response: I share the concern about incrementalism but come out differently. A 1e-18 uncertainty on its own would be a number, and I would not give a prize for it. What converts it into physics is that the clocks resolve the gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale sample, constrain constant drift, and show many-body spin effects, and none of that was available before the lattice. I would not rest the timing on the redefinition of the second, as it has not happened and the case does not need it. The case stands on the verified, independently reproduced invention and its measured consequences. I also noted your move from B050 to B009. Your own attribution caveat for B050 and the WMAP versus Planck and Puget question make me agree it is not ready, and I would keep it as a reserve only if that credit can be settled.

responses.point: Johansson notes that no departure from known physics has yet been seen with lattice clocks, while he ranks circuit QED first with a possible conflict, and keeps B010 and B008 as reserves.
responses.response: I accept that no violation of known physics has been observed, but the Physics Prize does not require one. It requires an original, verified invention that opens a door, and the lattice clock has done that. On your reserves, I do not think B008 can be the reserve now, both because of your own conflict note and because Wallraff's omission means the three names leave out someone who did the first strong-coupling experiment. I would support a recusal on B008 if it returns, as the chair asks, and I would not want that to cost you your say on B009. As to B010, I agree the science is sound. But Kroll and Lindroth are right that choosing three of four names is unresolved, and I am not yet sure that we have identified the right three from the original work.

responses.point: Kroll asks whether the redefinition of the second and the new-physics searches count as realised or prospective impact, and says he is relying on memory for the priority history.
responses.response: I would count them as partly realised and partly prospective, and I would say so. The redshift measurement and the constraints on constants and dark-matter couplings are published and reproducible. The redefinition and any new-physics signal are prospective, so the citation should not claim them. This keeps us consistent with the discovery-or-invention rule. I share your reliance on memory for the priority sequence, and I would hold us to the same standard. Your disclosure of a year in Hall's lab does not trouble me for B009, since you reported it openly and it is a loose link to the JILA environment and not to the lattice clock. I would ask that the committee note it in the record.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from B005 and from an opening rank of six, and records the risk that a widely expected prize crowds out candidates that are less well known to the committee.
responses.response: I take the crowding-out point seriously, and it is part of why I want us to argue from evidence and not from the eight-of-eight count. For B009 the evidence holds up on its own terms. I would not apply the same test to B005 on the same footing, though. You report that the confirmation of the Toner-Tu exponents is only partial, and Kroll doubts the quantitative confirmation, so I do not think it meets my bar of an experimentally verified original result yet. I would not hold B009 back for that reason. I would encourage the committee to keep your field's strongest experiments on the longlist for later years.

uncertainties: Whether an outside clock-metrology reviewer confirms that Katori's proposal and first demonstration, and Ye's lattice-clock accuracy milestones, are separable in the way colleagues describe, and that leaving out Lemonde, Ludlow, Oates, Takamoto and PTB is defensible.
How the full committee will weigh the 2005 and 2012 prizes. Eriksson and Pearce may still regard them as a reason to hold B009 back, and I cannot settle that for them.

Whether the citation can be worded so that it honours the lattice invention and its verified consequences without implying a prize for accuracy alone or for the not-yet-realised redefinition of the second.
Which reserve to name if B009 is set aside. B019 and B018 each have an open credit gap (Cao, and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang), and B010 requires choosing three of four names.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with Katori, Ye or the alternatives B019 and B018. My field is electron microscopy at Chalmers, and none of the credited people are co-authors or collaborators I am aware of. Göran Johansson is a Chalmers Physics colleague and has flagged his own possible conflict on B008. That is for him and the chair to settle, and it does not bear on B009. I note Kroll's disclosure of a year in John Hall's lab, which I do not consider disqualifying for B009. No change to my disclosure since round 1.
